items.q: Episodic vertigo for 2 hours with roaring tinnitus, fullness and fluctuating one ear deafness indicates what?
items.exp: Meniere disease from endolymphatic hydrops produces 20 minute to 12 hour vertigo attacks with fluctuating low frequency sensorineural loss, tinnitus and fullness. BPPV lasts seconds without hearing change.
r: Incorrect. BPPV spins for seconds on rolling, hearing normal.
Correct. Hours of vertigo with fluctuating ear symptoms is Meniere.
Incorrect. Labyrinthitis follows infection with constant days of vertigo and fixed loss.
Incorrect. Fistula vertigo is pressure triggered and brief.
items.kp: Minutes to hours spinning plus ear fullness equals Meniere.

items.q: Sudden 40 dB sensorineural loss over 2 days requires which urgent pathway?
o: Urgent audiometry, early steroid consideration and MRI meatus
items.exp: Sudden sensorineural loss is an emergency: prompt steroids within the early window improve recovery chances, and MRI excludes vestibular schwannoma or stroke. Wax would be conductive and visible.
r: Incorrect. Delay forfeits the treatment window.
Correct. Urgent confirmation, steroids and MRI.
Incorrect. Syringing treats canal wax, not cochlear loss.
Incorrect. Aid fitting waits for recovery plateau.
items.kp: Sudden deaf ear: days matter, scan and treat.

items.q: Slowly progressive unilateral sensorineural loss with tinnitus and poor speech discrimination needs exclusion of what?
items.exp: Retrocochlear tumours cause asymmetric sensorineural loss with disproportionately poor discrimination; gadolinium MRI of internal auditory meatus is mandatory. Conductive causes show air bone gaps instead.
r: Incorrect. Otosclerosis is conductive with good discrimination.
Correct. Exclude vestibular schwannoma by MRI.
Incorrect. Glue ear is conductive effusion.
Incorrect. Wax blocks canal visibly.
items.kp: One sided neural deafness: image the meatus.

items.q: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define which condition?
items.exp: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are diagnostic of NF2 (chromosome 22 merlin loss), with meningiomas and ependymomas. NF1 gives neurofibromas and cafe au lait spots instead.
r: Incorrect. NF1 is peripheral neurofibromas and skin signs.
Correct. Bilateral schwannomas mean NF2.
Incorrect. VHL gives haemangioblastomas and renal tumours.
Incorrect. Tuberous sclerosis gives cortical tubers and angiofibromas.

items.q: Noise induced hearing loss classically notches the audiogram where?
items.exp: Acoustic trauma injures basal hair cells tuned near 4 kHz (3 to 6 kHz range) producing the classic audiometric notch with later spread. Low frequencies survive until late damage.
r: Incorrect. Low frequencies are spared early.
Correct. Notch at 4 kHz is noise signature.
Incorrect. Bone and air fall together sensorineurally.
Incorrect. Highest tested tones also suffer with progression.
items.kp: Factory and gunfire carve the 4 kHz notch.

items.q: Aminoglycoside ototoxicity first damages hearing in which range and needs what monitoring?
items.exp: Ototoxins destroy basal outer hair cells first, so high frequency loss precedes speech range symptoms; baseline and serial high frequency audiometry (plus vestibular vigilance) monitor therapy.
r: Incorrect. Low tones fall late, and monitoring is essential.
Correct. High frequencies first with serial audiograms.
Incorrect. Speech range loss is late presentation.
Incorrect. Both conduction routes reflect cochlea.
items.kp: Ototoxins eat from the high tone base upward: monitor.

items.q: Vertigo provoked by loud sounds (Tullio phenomenon) suggests which lesion?
items.exp: A bony dehiscence creates a third window so sound and pressure move endolymph causing brief vertigo and autophony, confirmed on fine cut CT and vestibular evoked potentials. Plugging surgery helps severe cases.
r: Incorrect. Crystals trigger position, not sound.
Correct. Sound induced vertigo means canal dehiscence.
Incorrect. Meniere attacks are spontaneous and prolonged.
Incorrect. Otosclerosis deafens conductively without sound vertigo.
items.kp: Loud sound makes world tilt: third window leak.

o: Bilateral symmetric high frequency sensorineural loss
items.exp: Ageing cochlear loss is bilateral, symmetric and high frequency sloping, impairing consonant discrimination especially in noise. Unilateral or fluctuating patterns demand other diagnoses.
r: Incorrect. Unilateral loss needs retrocochlear exclusion.
Correct. Symmetric high frequency slope of ageing.
Incorrect. No air bone gap in cochlear ageing.
Incorrect. Fluctuating low loss is Meniere pattern.
items.kp: Old ears lose high tones on both sides together.

items.q: BPPV is distinguished from Meniere primarily how?
o: Vertigo seconds triggered by rolling, normal hearing
items.exp: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo gives seconds long spins on rolling or looking up, positive Dix Hallpike, treated by Epley repositioning, with normal hearing. Meniere attacks last far longer with ear symptoms.
r: Correct. Brief positional spins, normal hearing: BPPV.
Incorrect. Days of vertigo with deafness is labyrinthitis.
Incorrect. Those are Meniere auditory features.
Incorrect. Fever points to infectious labyrinth disease.
items.kp: Seconds on rolling equals crystals, hours with fullness equals Meniere.

items.q: Autoimmune inner ear disease typically progresses how and responds to what?
o: Bilateral over weeks to months; corticosteroids
items.exp: Immune mediated cochlear injury progresses bilaterally over weeks to months (too slow for sudden loss, too fast for ageing) and often stabilises with corticosteroids, needing rheumatologic co care.
r: Incorrect. Decades unilateral suggests tumour pathway.
Correct. Bilateral subacute progression answering steroids.
Incorrect. Antibiotics treat infectious labyrinthitis.
Incorrect. Congenital loss is non progressive pattern.
items.kp: Both ears worsening over weeks: think immune, try steroids.
